name: Cue-Dependent Forgetting
description: People can fail to retrieve information not because it is gone, but because the cue available at recall does not match the cue under which it was encoded. Memory often looks lost when the route back into it is missing.
design_relevance_note: Thin but real relevance: reminder systems, return-to-task flows, search labels, saved-state cues, and recognition-heavy interfaces work better when they recreate or preserve the cues present when the user first learned or stored something. This is more a memory-support principle than a mainstream day-to-day UX law.
prevalence_note: A standard term in memory psychology, but rarely named explicitly in mainstream digital-product design compared with the more directly design-facing recognition-vs-recall heuristic.

findings.description: A review and meta-analysis concluded that memory retrieval can improve when the original environmental context is reinstated at test, supporting context-dependent memory as a real if condition-sensitive retrieval effect.
findings.source_title: Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis

findings.description: Across episodic-memory experiments, Tulving and Thomson showed that recall depends on overlap between encoding and retrieval cues: information can appear forgotten when the cue available at test does not match the cue under which it was encoded.
findings.source_title: Encoding specificity and retrieval processes in episodic memory.

findings.description: An fMRI study found that different brain regions correlate with successful later memory depending on which cognitive process (social impression-formation vs. nonsocial sequencing) was engaged during initial encoding -- direct neural evidence for encoding specificity: what gets encoded, and how well it can later be retrieved, depends on the specific mental operation performed at study time, not just exposure to the material. Independently extends the encoding-specificity/cue-dependent-forgetting mechanism into a neuroimaging paradigm and a social-cognition domain, using a completely different method than Tulving & Thomson's original 1973 behavioral demonstration.
findings.source_title: Encoding-Specific Effects of Social Cognition on the Neural Correlates of Subsequent Memory
